lines: James Gleick, discussing his new book The Telephone: A New History, argues that transformative technologies are ultimately defined by their users, not their inventors.

He rejects the lone-genius story of the telephone: it came out of a messy, competitive field of simultaneous inventors, and early users such as farmers stringing calls over barbed-wire fences turned it from a broadcast device into a tool for casual conversation.
The telephone was the original network-effect business; Gleick says the Bell monopoly, which funded Bell Labs, was the result of strategic consolidation rather than something progress required.
He credits Bell Labs' output to combining wide intellectual freedom with a clear overarching mission.
Gleick sees AI as a continuation of the digital revolution rather than a discontinuous 'fourth industrial revolution', with computers simply tackling ever more abstract problems.
title: From the Telephone to Modern Computing | James Gleick
